OVERVIEW

[
1
]

R. S. (
R.
)
[1]

seeks the homologation of the protection mandate of her mother, the Concerned
Person M. A. (
Ms. A.
). She also claims from her brother, D. S. (
D.
),
the reimbursement to her mother of $ 48,000 that the latter transferred to
D..

[
2
]

Ms. A.’s incapacity is not contested by the
parties. Indeed, the medical and psychosocial reports confirm that she is
totally and permanently incapable of protecting her person and administering
her property.
[2]

[
3
]

However, D. contests the homologation of the protection
mandate on the following basis: First, that his mother lacked the capacity to
sign it; second, that she was unduly influenced by R. into appointing her as
sole mandatary to Ms. A.’s person and property.
[3]

Regarding the request for reimbursement of $48,000, D. states that his mother
gave him these amounts as a gift. Moreover, he performed work on her properties,
the value of which is roughly equivalent to the amount given to him by his
mother. Accordingly, he should not be required to reimburse the money and if he
is, restitution is owed to him by his mother for the work that he performed.

[
4
]

For the reasons that follow, the Court
homologates the Protection Mandate and condemns D. to pay his mother the amount
of $48,000.

FACTS

[
5
]

Ms. A. is presently 91 years old. She was born
in Italy and moved to Town A around 1955. In 1957, she married H. S., who died
in 2009.

[
6
]

At the time of the hearing, Ms. A. owned three
properties near each other in Town B. She occupies one floor of her duplex
located at [Address 1].

[
7
]

D. lives next door to Ms. A. in her property
located at [Address 2]. R. lives at [Address 3], in another property owned by Ms.
A.. D. and R. do not pay rent. According to R., they live rent free in exchange
for being responsible for all maintenance and repairs, such as roofing,
property and school taxes and insurance.

[
8
]

D. personally owns a property at [Address 4]
near his mother and sister, which he rents out to tenants.

[
9
]

Until the summer of 2015, R. and D. regularly saw
their mother, though R. took a more active role in helping her mother manage
her affairs. D. testified he
would “do the work that he could do” which included cutting the grass, pruning
trees and changing doors and windows. He confirmed that R. helped Ms. A. with her
finances.

[
10
]

However, in the summer of 2015, Ms. A. mandated
a lawyer to write to D. following his request that she transfer one of her
properties to him. Neither the letter nor its content were produced in
evidence, but both R. and D. testified that, as a result of the letter, as well
as events that will be more fully set out below, D. did not resume seeing his
mother regularly until 2018.

[
11
]

R. described her mother as a “proud Italian
woman”, independent, bossy and with a bit of a temper. Until the onset of her
dementia, she took pride in the way she looked and was always “dressed to the
nines”.

[
12
]

In early 2016, Ms. A. would visit her late
husband’s sister, who was suffering from Alzheimer’s Disease and was living at
home. Ms. A. expressed to R. that in the event she became incapable, she wanted
to be similarly cared for in her home.

[
13
]

To that end, she decided to modify her
protection mandate to express this wish. Her previous mandate dated from 2006
or 2007, prior to her husband’s death. R. told Ms. A. she would have to contact
the notary to make this change. Ms. A. asked R. to make the appointment and
drive her there. R. contacted Notary Suzanne Lamarre, who had taken over the
practice of Ms. A. and her husband’s previous notary. Eventually, a meeting
with the notary would take place in April of 2016.

[
14
]

In the meantime, on February 7, 2016,
[4]
there was an incident at the
supermarket. According to R., D. approached her and started yelling at her.
[5]
He picked up a glass bottle
and threatened to hit her with it but then backed away. However, at the check
out, he charged at R., accused her of taking his money and he also grabbed Ms. A.
by her lapels.

[
15
]

In his testimony, D. denied having touched his
mother but confirmed he took a glass jar, held it up, but did not swing, at R..
[6]
When he saw her again at the
check out, he “went black and lost it” and started calling her names. He stated
that he did not call his mother names or threaten her.

[
16
]

Ms. A. and R. reported the incident to the
police and D. was arrested. A restraining order was obtained prohibiting D.
from communicating or approaching either R. or Ms. A..
[7]
In December 2016, D. signed a
peace bond for a duration of one year in accordance with
Article 810
of the
Criminal
Code
and was acquitted.
[8]

Accordingly, from February 11, 2016, the date of the restraining order, to
approximately December 2017, he had no communication or contact with either R.
or Ms. A..

[
17
]

The first meeting with M
tre
Lamarre
was on April 14, 2016. According to R., M
tre
Lamarre was accompanied
by her colleague, M
tre
De Riggi, but M
tre
Lamarre led the
meeting. Ms. A. explained to M
tre
Lamarre that in the event of her
incapacity, she wanted to remain at home as long as possible.
[9]

[
18
]

M
tre
Lamarre asked Ms. A. who she
wanted to appoint as her mandatary. Ms. A. replied that she wanted R. to
be her mandatary since R. was already helping her with visits to the doctor,
rent collection and groceries.

[
19
]

R. testified that M
tre
Lamarre then
asked Ms. A. who she wanted to appoint as her substitute mandatary. Ms. A.
did not want it to be D. considering the supermarket incident. R. suggested
various family members and some of R.’s friends. Ms. A. eventually said she
would agree to Linda Viviani, a friend of R.’s from elementary school whom Ms. A.
has also known for decades. R. left the meeting for about 15 minutes to call Ms. Viviani
to ask her if she would agree to be the substitute mandatary. She was reluctant
but nonetheless agreed.

[
20
]

R. testified that during the meeting, the notary
spoke to her mother in French and English, both of which her mother spoke and
understood in addition to her native Italian. M
tre
Lamarre testified
that the meeting was conducted in English. She stated that Ms. A. was clear in
her instructions and since she had no doubt as to her capacity, she did not
feel it was necessary to require a letter from her doctor confirming that she
had the capacity to change her mandate, as is M
tre
Lamarre’s
practice in some cases. The meeting lasted 45 minutes to one hour.
[10]

[
21
]

On April 26, 2018, R. drove Ms. A. to M
tre

Lamarre’s office to sign the protection mandate. M
tre
Lamarre
reviewed the mandate with Ms. A. in the presence of M
tre
De Riggi.
According to R., it was read and explained to Ms. A. in English, French
and Italian.
[11]

M
tre
Lamarre testified it was reviewed in English, which is the
language of the mandate. Ms. A. confirmed she agreed with its contents and she
signed it.

[
22
]

Following the signature of the mandate, Ms. A.
continued with her regular activities, which included doing her errands, her
banking, her groceries, seeing her doctor every three months to check her blood
pressure, taking the bus and metro to visit her sister in Town C and shopping
at specialty stores on St-Laurent Boulevard.

[
23
]

In September 2017, R. noticed that her mother
was repeating her stories and becoming forgetful. She accompanied Ms. A. to her
next doctor’s appointment and advised the doctor. He referred Ms. A. to Dr. Elise
Levinoff at the Jewish General Hospital.

[
24
]

In February 2018, Ms. A. had her first appointment
with Dr. Levinoff. A series of tests confirmed that she was in the early stages
of dementia. Medication was prescribed and a follow-up appointment was
scheduled for six months later.

[
25
]

However, R. noticed a serious deterioration over
the next few months, evidenced by her mother crossing her busy street in the
middle of traffic and assuming the cars would stop for her, forgetting to eat
and decreased hygiene. This was particularly striking to R. given her mother’s
usual pride in her appearance. R. brought Ms. A. back to see Dr. Levinoff in
May 2018. By then, Ms. A. had lost 11 pounds. Dr. Levinoff increased Ms. A.’s
medication.

[
26
]

In her report dated June 21, 2018, Dr. Levinoff
confirmed that Ms. A. was totally and permanently incapable of protecting her
person and administering her property.
[12]

Dr. Levinoff advised R. that she should initiate homologation proceedings.

[
27
]

Sometime in July 2018, Ms. A. told R. that she
had gone to the bank with D. “to see how much was in the account”. D. testified
that in July, he spoke to his mother outside by the fence between their homes.
[13]
He told her he had financial problems. She replied that she wanted
to give him $ 100,000. In 2012, she had given him $ 90,000. This
time, he told her he would think about it and he subsequently accepted.

[
28
]

On September 4, they went to the Royal Bank.
[14]
According to D., when Ms. A. told the teller she wanted to withdraw
$100,000, the teller replied that he could only give her $ 6,000. When D.
asked why she could not have $100,000, the teller replied that it was
confidential. D. confirmed that he received $6,000 that day.
[15]

[
29
]

They went back to the Royal Bank on October 2
and D. received another $6,000.
[16]
It
appears that he told the bank that Ms. A. needed money to live.
[17]
Shortly before each $6,000 withdrawal, $6,000 was deposited into
the account with the notation “Misc Payment TFSA”. Following the withdrawals,
each time there was a balance left in the account of about $25.

[
30
]

On October 9, October 31 and November 27, 2018, D.
received additional amounts from his mother’s CIBC account of $3,000, $8,000
and $25,000.
[18]

[
31
]

D. admits to having received a total of $48,000.
He testified that he needed this money to pay his debts.

[
32
]

On December 14, 2018, R. obtained a court order
protecting Ms. A.’s property.
[19]

On February 13, 2019, R. instituted the present proceeding to homologate the
protection mandate. It was subsequently modified to request the reimbursement
of $48,000 from D..

ISSUES

[
33
]

The questions to be resolved are the following:

33.1.

Was Ms. A. capable of signing the protection
mandate dated April 26, 2016?

33.2.

Was Ms. A. unduly influenced by R. into signing
the protection mandate dated April 26, 2016?

33.3.

Is the homologation of the protection mandate in the interest of Ms.
A., will it respect her rights and will it safeguard her autonomy, taking into
account her wishes and preferences
?

33.4.

Should D. be condemned to reimburse $48,000 to Ms.
A.?

ANALYSIS

1.

Was
Ms. A. capable of signing the protection mandate dated April 26, 2016
?

[
34
]

Ms. A. had the capacity to sign the protection mandate.

[
35
]

Since capacity is presumed,
[20]
D. has the burden of proving that
his mother lacked the capacity to sign the mandate by establishing “
l’existence
d’un état habituel

d’aliénation ou de faiblesse d’esprit
”.
[21]
This must be proven on a
balance of probabilities and a simple doubt is not sufficient to meet this
burden.
[22]

[
36
]

D. has not adduced any evidence of even a doubt
as to Ms. A.’s capacity at the time she signed her protection mandate. While he
was in regular contact with his mother at least until the summer of 2015, he did
not testify about any issues with respect to Ms. A.’s cognition.

[
37
]

In fact, in her argument, D.’s attorney did not
make any representations on this issue.

[
38
]

The protection mandate was signed on April 26,
2016. According to R., the first sign of any problem with Ms. A.’s cognitive
function was in September 2017. Prior to that, there is no evidence that she
exhibited any cognitive problems.

[
39
]

M
tre
Lamarre testified that she had
no doubt of Ms. A.’s capacity to understand the protection mandate.

[
40
]

Accordingly, the Court finds that Ms. A. had the
capacity to sign the protection mandate.

2.

Did
R. exercise undue influence (
captation
) over Ms. A. in regard to the
signature of the protection mandate
?

[
41
]

R. did not exercise undue influence over Ms. A..

[
42
]

D. has the burden of proving that R. unduly influenced
their mother.
[23]

[
43
]

In a leading case on undue influence,
Stoneham
and Tewkesbury v. Ouellet
, the Supreme Court of Canada set out the test for
undue influence. It is akin to fraud that vitiates the consent of the party who
has been influenced. It is characterized by alienation of the concerned person
from her relatives, it is done by the influencer in her own interest and by
abusing her position over the concerned person’s mind. The influencing person
may resort to slander and seek to alienate the concerned person’s affection for
other family members.
[24]

[
44
]

In
Savoie
.
c.
Savoie
, the Court
cites Professor Brière as follows on this subject:

“Les faits de captation deviennent
cependant dolosifs lorsqu’ils s’accompagnent de pratiques artificieuses, comme
l’interception de la correspondance ou le fait d’écarter les visites ou encore
le dénigrement systématique à l’adresse des proches parents. Encore faut-il que
les manœuvres frauduleuses aient été déterminantes du consentement; pour
apprécier ce caractère déterminant, il faut tenir compte de la résistance que
le testateur était capable d’offrir dans les circonstances, e.g. alors que ses
facultés étaient affaiblies par la maladie.”
[25]

[
45
]

The reasonableness or unreasonableness of the
clauses of the mandate will also be relevant.
[26]

[
46
]

Undue influence is difficult to prove because it
is often done in secret. For this reason, evidence can be made by presumption, proving
facts that are sufficiently serious, precise and concordant to permit the
drawing of an inference of undue influence from those established facts.
[27]

[
47
]

D. has not met his burden of proof to establish
undue influence.

[
48
]

First, D. has adduced no evidence, by
presumption or otherwise, to support his allegation of undue influence by R..
He told the social worker that R.’s conduct could be considered “elder abuse”
but “he did not want to share specifics stating that he would address them in
Court”.
[28]

[
49
]

At trial, his only testimony on this issue was the
vague statement that his mother told him that she felt threatened by R. and
that R. became angry with their mother in 2019 (three years
after
the
mandate was signed) when she answered the door to a stranger and spent $ 700
on pillows being sold by the salesman who rang the doorbell. R. explained in
her testimony that she was concerned for her mother’s safety because her mother
had opened the door to a stranger.

[
50
]

Second, undue influence often occurs in the
context of relationships with elderly, vulnerable people. While Ms. A. is
elderly, there is no evidence that she was particularly vulnerable at the time
the protection mandate was signed in 2016.

[
51
]

Third, Ms. A. was the one who initiated the
process to change her mandate. Her decision was initially motivated by her wish
to add a clause about living arrangements. R.’s testimony about this is
confirmed by M
tre
Lamarre’s testimony and by the mandate itself.
[29]

[
52
]

At the time of the first meeting with M
tre

Lamarre, D. was the subject of a restraining order and could not communicate
with his mother following the supermarket incident. It was therefore reasonable
that Ms. A. decided not to appoint him as her mandatary. As for the appointment
of R.’s friend Linda Viviani as the substitute mandatary, Ms. A. had known her
for years. Furthermore, no evidence was adduced to show that Linda Viviani was
an inappropriate choice.

[
53
]

Fourth, although R. was present for all but 15
minutes of the first meeting, M
tre
Lamarre testified that she had no
concerns about Ms. A.’s capacity. Although capacity and undue influence, though
sometimes related, are not the same, M
tre
Lamarre’s testimony confirms
that she noted nothing of concern regarding R.’s presence. Furthermore, her
presence at this meeting was not unusual since R. was already involved in her
mother’s affairs, which was admitted by D..

[
54
]

The Court briefly questioned Ms. A.. She did not
express any fear of either R. or D..

[
55
]

Accordingly, the Court concludes that R. did not
exercise undue influence on Ms. A. in relation to the change in the latter’s protection
mandate.

3.

Is
the homologation of the protection mandate in the interest of Ms. A., will it
respect her rights and will it safeguard her autonomy, taking into account her
wishes and preferences
?

[
56
]

The homologation of the protection mandate is in
the interest of Ms. A., it respects her rights and it will safeguard her
autonomy, including by taking into account her wishes and preferences.

[
57
]

As stated above, Ms. A.’s total and permanent
incapacity has been established.
[30]

[
58
]

Prior to her incapacity, Ms. A. set out her
wishes and preferences in her protection mandate.
[31]

[
59
]

The psychosocial report confirms that Ms. A.
requires assistance due to her poor short-term and variable long-term memory,
her variable disorientation to time, poor judgment, poor problem solving and
limited insight. After speaking with the parties, as well as Dr. Levinoff, Ms. A.’s
sister and her niece, the social worker concluded that it is in Ms. A.’s best
interest that her mandate be homologated and that R. be appointed mandatary to
her mother’s person and property.
[32]

[
60
]

Appointing R. is indeed in Ms. A.’s interest. Even
prior to her incapacity, R. regularly helped her mother with her affairs. For
example, she would drive her to some appointments, write cheques for her mother
to sign, she renegotiated the insurance for the properties and she managed roof
repairs.

[
61
]

In September 2017, upon observing changes in Ms.
A.’s cognition, R. acted quickly, going with Ms. A. to her next doctor’s
appointment to advise the doctor and seek advice. R. took Ms. A. to see Dr.
Levinoff in February 2018 and when Ms. A.’s cognition declined rapidly, R.
moved up her mother’s appointment to investigate the situation.

[
62
]

Upon questioning by the Court, Ms. A. did not
remember having signed the protection mandate. She stated that both her son and
daughter help her, particularly by bringing her meals or taking her to
restaurants, but that she does not need help.
[33]

She confirmed that someone comes to clean her house.

[
63
]

R. testified that she wants “the best care
possible” for her mother so that she can remain at home, in her garden, near
her children, with help that she can afford. R. “wants her mother to be happy
and to get what she needs”.

[
64
]

The Court believes that R. will ensure the moral
and material well-being of Ms. A., taking into account her condition, her needs
and her faculties as well as the other circumstances of her situation.
[34]

[
65
]

Accordingly, Ms. A.’s protection mandate should
be homologated and R. should be appointed as mandatary to her mother’s person
and property.

4.

Should
D. be condemned to reimburse $ 48,000 to Ms. A.
?

[
66
]

D. shall be condemned to reimburse $ 48,000
to Ms. A..

4.1

Characterization
of the contract

[
67
]

The Court concludes that the contract(s) in
question is a gift.

[
68
]

A gift is a contract by gratuitous title,
[35]
which means that one party,
in this case Ms. A., obligated herself to the other, D., for his benefit and
without Ms. A. obtaining any advantage in return.
[36]

[
69
]

D. testified that his mother did not want the
money she gave him to be returned to her. He stated that at some point
following her offer to give him $ 100,000, he told her that he would do
some work on her properties and give her a tax receipt for the work.
[37]
He described this as a
condition that he proposed but that she did not request.

[
70
]

Since the evidence is that Ms. A. paid money
from her bank accounts to D. with no expectation that it would be reimbursed
and without requesting anything from D. in return, the Court concludes that the
payments to D. are contracts of gift.

4.2

Annulment of the gifts

[
71
]

In a contract, the contracting party, in this
case Ms. A., must have the requisite capacity to contract.
[38]
The evidence is clear that as
of June 21, 2018, she was incapable of administering her property.
[39]
Regarding this issue, the
medical report issued on that date states that Ms. A. “has demonstrated
difficulties with calculations and cannot manage her day-to-day finances and
complex assets. She has poor judgment and insight into this and needs
assistance/supervision.”
[40]

[
72
]

No evidence was adduced by D. regarding his
mother’s conduct or capacity at the relevant time that would contradict this
conclusion.

[
73
]

Article 2170 C.C.Q. provides as follows:

2170. Acts performed before the
homologation of the mandate may be annulled or the resulting obligations may be
reduced, on the mere proof that the mandator’s incapacity was notorious or
known to the other contracting party at the time that the acts were entered
into.

Acts performed alone by the
mandator after the homologation of the mandate that are incompatible with its
stipulations may not be annulled or the resulting obligations reduced, unless
he suffers injury therefrom.

[
74
]

If Ms. A.’s incapacity was notorious or known to
D., then the gifts may be annulled.

[
75
]

To be notorious, the incapacity must be
generally known by a large number of people.
[41]

The evidence does not establish that Ms. A.’s incapacity was notorious.

[
76
]

However, the Court concludes that the serious,
precise and concordant facts in evidence
[42]

lead to the presumption that D. was aware of his mother’s incapacity at the
time the gifts were made.

[
77
]

D. was not a credible witness. He argued that
his mother lacked the capacity in April 2016 to understand her protection
mandate. On the other hand, he took the position that his mother had the
capacity in 2018 to gift him $100,000. These two positions cannot co-exist and
they undermine D.’s credibility regarding this issue.

[
78
]

In describing his mother when his father was
alive, D. stated that she would go to the bank and pay bills but that she did
not know how much money she had and only cared that it was safe in the bank. If
he believed that she was unaware of her finances when she had capacity, why
would he believe that she understood the implications of offering to give him
$100,000?

[
79
]

In other words, when it was convenient for D. to
posit that his mother lacked capacity, or at minimum financial knowledge, such
as in relation to the signature of her 2016 mandate, he did so. When it was
inconvenient, such as when claiming that the gifts are valid, he changed his
position.

[
80
]

The June 2018 medical report states that “the
patient has moderate mixed dementia and is demonstrating difficulties managing
her finances independently. Therefore, because of her poor short term memory,
she requires assistance”.
[43]

The report continues: “She requires assistance for instrumental activities of
daily living and needs reminders to perform her basic activities of daily
living”.

[
81
]

D. testified that he did not notice anything
different about Ms. A. in July 2018, although he had not seen her very much in
the previous two to three years. When she was well, Ms. A. was described as a
woman who took great care and pride in her appearance. By the summer of 2018,
she had lost significant weight and often looked unkept.
[44]
It is not credible that D. failed
to notice these changes and question the situation.

[
82
]

Furthermore, D. testified that when they visited
the bank on September 4, the teller would not let Ms. A. withdraw or transfer
$100,000 and limited the transaction to $6,000. He testified that the teller
would not explain the refusal, but this should have also been cause for concern
for D..

[
83
]

Rather than questioning the situation further, or
contacting his sister, D. instead took his mother to a different bank and obtained
$8,000 from her CIBC account on October 31, 2018, and $25,000 from the same
account on November 27, 2018.
[45]

Both these amounts exceed the $6,000 limit imposed by the Royal Bank, of which D.
was aware.

[
84
]

In the summer of 2018, all the signs pointed
toward Ms. A.’s incapacity. These factors lead the Court to draw the inference
[46]
that D. would have been aware
that his mother lacked the capacity to administer her property and gift him $100,000,
$48,000 of which he in fact received.

[
85
]

The contracts of gift shall be annulled.

4.3

Restitution

[
86
]

Article 1422(2)
C.C.Q.
provides
that when a contract is annulled, each party
is bound to restore to the other the prestation he has received
.

[
87
]

D. argues that if the contracts of gift are
annulled, he is entitled to restitution pursuant to Article 1706
C.C.Q.

which reads as follows:

Art. 1706. Minors and persons of
full age under tutorship or under a protection mandate are bound to make
restitution of prestations only to the extent of the enrichment they retain
from them; proof of such enrichment is borne by the person claiming restitution.

They may,
however, be bound to make full restitution where restitution has become
impossible through their intentional or gross fault.

[
88
]

Article 1706 C.C.Q. does not apply to this
situation for the following reasons.

[
89
]

Restitution of prestation takes place where a
person is bound by law to return the property she has received under a contract
which is subsequently annulled.
[47]

[
90
]

In the present case, Ms. A. did not receive any
property under the contracts of gift so there is nothing for her to give back.
[48]

[
91
]

D. testified that at some point following his
mother’s offer to give him $100,000, he told her that he would do some work on
her properties and give her a tax receipt for the work.
[49]

[
92
]

D. was free to perform this work but since it
was not requested by his mother and was not an obligation under the contract,
it cannot form the basis of a claim for restitution.

[
93
]

Even if Article 1706 C.C.Q
.
applied,
which the Court finds is not the case, D. had the burden of proving Ms. A.’s
enrichment and he has failed to do so.

[
94
]

D. testified that from July 2018 to November
2018, he worked “morning and night…weekends also…7:30 am to sundown” though his
description of the work was vague and it was not always clear if he was working
on his residence or his mother’s. He stated that he cut the grass, pruned the
trees and shrubs, scraped the stairs at his mother’s residence, worked on a
retaining wall, painted some planters at his residence (owned by his mother),
and he did some exterior work and drainage at [Address 5].

[
95
]

In January 2019, D. gave his mother three
identical documents dated respectively December 1, 2018, December 1, 2019 and
December 1 2020
[50]

that each stated: “I D. S. received 15000.00 from mrs Ms. A. – S. for work
preformed during the year of ____” (
sic
), with each year inserted and
his social insurance number on the bottom.

[
96
]

At the time that he gave his mother these
documents, D. had already been served with the Motion to Protect the Property
of the Respondent before the Imminent Proceedings for the Homologation of the
Protection Mandate in CS 500-17-105-921-186.

[
97
]

It goes without saying that the statements on
the documents are not true since D. received $48,000 in 2018, not $15,000 in
each of 2018, 2019 and 2020. Furthermore, the statements for December 2019 and
2020 were provided in January 2019.

[
98
]

D. testified that he did not finish the work he
started and for the most part, what he described was performed in 2018.

[
99
]

R. sent the 2018 receipt to her mother’s
accountant. D. filed copies of Ms. A.’s statements of building expenses and tax
returns for the years 2018, 2019 and 2020
[51]

but no evidence was adduced to establish the tax benefit to Ms. A. of claiming
the amounts on the 2018 receipt.

[
100
]

R. did not claim the expenses from 2019 and 2020
on her mother’s tax returns because she was not aware of any work having been
done by D. in those years.

[
101
]

There is minimal evidence of any work performed
in 2019 and 2020. There are no time sheets to confirm the number of hours and
no photos of the work he performed in any of the years in question. Though D.
frequently stated during his testimony that such photos existed, they were not
adduced into evidence.

[
102
]

D. testified that he claimed the amounts for
2018, 2019 and 2020 on his taxes though there was no documentary evidence produced
to support this.

[
103
]

Considering the above, D. failed to establish
the value of the enrichment that his mother received from the work that he
performed on her properties.

[
104
]

Accordingly, even if the Court had concluded
that the provisions on restitution applied, no restitution would be owed to
him.

CONCLUSION

[
105
]

Considering the above, the Court concludes that Ms.
A.’s protection mandate should be homologated, R. should be appointed mandatary
to her mother’s person and property and D. should be condemned to reimburse
$48,000 to his mother.

[
106
]

As for legal costs, D. shall be ordered to pay
legal costs but not expert fees. This is because the medical and psycho-social
reports are required in all applications to homologate protection mandates,
whether or not they are contested. Since D. did not contest the issue of his
mother’s capacity at the time of trial and he did not file any
counter-expertise, it is appropriate that Ms. A. bear the cost of those
reports, as she would have had the application been uncontested.
